words.technical: The composite trend score is mildly positive at about 0.15, but it is an average of disagreeing horizons: the three-month and twelve-month readings are clearly positive while the one-month and six-month readings are negative. Range position near 0.41 puts spot just below the midpoint of the past year's range, so there is room in both directions before the market is testing an extreme. Daily volatility around 1.4% is what widens the one-week band to roughly seven percent either side of the base. The model holds a Flat stance and would flip to Hold above roughly 4513, with the confidence figure reflecting the historically strong hit rate of Flat stances rather than any conviction about direction.
words.macro: The Fed's quarter-point hike to 3.75%-4.00% and its signal of more to come would ordinarily be a headwind, but gold ended the week marginally higher after three consecutive weekly declines, as falling crude prices blunted the hawkish message. Core PCE inflation has accelerated from 3.0% in December 2025 to 3.3% in July 2026, which keeps a real-rate argument alive on both sides: higher nominal yields weigh, but persistent inflation supports the hedge case. The frozen calendar puts the August PCE print on 30 September and the September CPI on 14 October, both of which fall inside the one-month horizon and are the obvious repricing points.
words.long_term: Gold's structural bid has rested on official-sector accumulation and demand for a reserve asset outside any single currency, and neither of those depends on the near-term rate path. The standing risk to that picture is a sustained period of positive real yields that raises the cost of holding a non-yielding asset.

eoy_scenarios.central: The central band assumes the current tension persists without resolving: sticky inflation holds the hedging bid while higher policy rates cap advances, leaving spot oscillating around present levels into the turn of the year.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The upside case needs one of two things — inflation that fails to respond to tightening, forcing a real-rate decline, or a growth or geopolitical shock that revives safe-haven demand faster than yields can offset it.
eoy_scenarios.downside: The downside case is the clean, orthodox one: the Fed follows through on further hikes, inflation cools toward target, real yields rise and the metal loses its comparative advantage against cash.

words.technical: The trend composite sits just under 0.18, a shade firmer than the precious-metals complex average, and carries the same internal disagreement: strongly positive over twelve months and three months, negative over one and six. Range position near 0.30 is the lowest of the seven instruments, placing spot in the bottom third of its own twelve-month range despite a gain of close to four percent on the week. Daily volatility of roughly 2.5% is nearly double gold's and is the reason the one-week band spans about fifteen percent end to end. The stance is Flat, flipping to Hold near 69.88 — a level the week's rally has left within reach.
words.macro: Silver hit a weekly high as the pullback in crude reopened the path for metals after the Fed's hike. The metal's dual character is doing the work here: it is priced partly as a monetary hedge alongside gold and partly as an industrial input into electronics and solar manufacturing, which makes it more sensitive than gold to both rate expectations and the growth outlook. With the August PCE report due 30 September and September CPI on 14 October, the same inflation prints that move gold will move silver, typically with a larger amplitude.
words.long_term: Silver's structural story rests on industrial demand from electrification and solar deployment meeting a supply base that is largely a by-product of other mining and therefore slow to respond to price. That combination argues for a market that is chronically tight but also violently cyclical, since the industrial half of demand falls away in a downturn exactly when the monetary half is most needed.

eoy_scenarios.central: The central band reflects continued two-sided pull: monetary demand tracking gold, industrial demand steady, and neither dominant enough to break the range into year-end.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The upside case is a precious-metals rally in which silver's higher beta does what it usually does, amplified by any evidence of physical tightness in industrial supply chains.
eoy_scenarios.downside: The downside case combines a successful disinflation that strips out the monetary premium with a manufacturing slowdown that cuts the industrial bid at the same time — the scenario in which silver's two demand sources fail together rather than offsetting.

words.technical: Crude carries the strongest trend composite in the set at roughly 0.58, and unusually for this week it is coherent across horizons: one-month, three-month and twelve-month readings are all firmly positive, with only the six-month read flat. Range position near 0.70 keeps spot in the upper third of the past year's range even after a weekly fall of more than four and a half percent, which tells you how much ground was gained before the retreat. Daily volatility of about 3.3% is the highest of the seven instruments and produces easily the widest bands. The stance is Hold, flipping to Flat near 91.83 — close enough that another week like this one would take it there.
words.macro: The week's decline was an unwinding of fear rather than a change in fundamentals. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which carries crude to the Red Sea and bypasses the Strait of Hormuz, was shut after drone strikes from inside Iraq, and the market spent the prior week pricing a prolonged outage. Prices fell back as US officials said the line would restart within days and as Saudi Arabia raised ship-to-ship transfers outside Hormuz — selling as much as 60 million barrels for September and October loadings that way — to keep exports flowing. The disagreement that matters is over repair time: officials describe an interruption measured in days, while independent analysts reading satellite imagery of the damaged pumping station and regional officials both suggest weeks, which leaves a live two-sided risk into the coming week.
words.long_term: Crude's structural picture is one of a market with thin spare capacity and heavy dependence on a small number of chokepoints, so the risk premium is episodic rather than steady and can be added or removed in days. Against that sits the slower drift of electrification and efficiency on the demand side, which caps the durability of any supply-driven advance.

eoy_scenarios.central: The central band assumes the pipeline is repaired on something like the expected schedule, Gulf exports normalise and prices settle back toward the level that prevailed before the strike, with the geopolitical premium thinning but not disappearing.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The upside case is a repair that runs to the weeks-long end of estimates, or a second disruption to export infrastructure, either of which restores the scarcity premium against a market with little slack.
eoy_scenarios.downside: The downside case is a quick restart combined with a demand response to tighter monetary policy — higher rates slowing activity into year-end just as the supply scare fades.

Range position near 0.59 is just above the midpoint of the past year. Daily volatility of about 2.4% is high in absolute terms but, notably, below crude's this week. words.macro: Bitcoin gained more than five percent on the week, with most of it arriving in the final sessions as markets moved past the Fed decision and a regulatory development lifted sentiment: the SEC's move to open up tokenised share trading was read as a constructive signal for market-structure reform. That followed a setback earlier in the week when the Senate narrowly blocked the CLARITY Act, which briefly pushed prices below 76,000 before they recovered. The pattern worth noting is that the asset absorbed a legislative disappointment and a rate hike in the same week and still finished materially higher, which says more about the current bid than either headline does on its own.
words.long_term: The standing structural question is whether the asset behaves as a scarce monetary alternative or as a high-beta risk asset, and the historical record shows it switching between the two depending on the liquidity regime. A tightening cycle is the environment in which the risk-asset reading has usually dominated.

eoy_scenarios.central: The central band assumes the regulatory drip continues to be mildly constructive without a decisive legislative outcome, and that liquidity conditions tighten gradually rather than abruptly — leaving a wide but unresolved range into year-end.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The upside case needs a genuine structural catalyst, such as the market-structure legislation that failed this week returning in a passable form, or a clear pivot back toward easier policy.
eoy_scenarios.downside: The downside case is a tightening cycle that runs further than markets expect, draining risk appetite, with no legislative progress to offset it.

words.technical: This is the week's most interesting disagreement. The trend composite is the highest of any instrument at roughly 0.69, driven by very strong six- and twelve-month readings, and range position of about 0.90 puts the index near the top of its own twelve-month range — yet the one-month reading has turned negative and the index was fractionally lower on the week. Daily volatility of around 0.65% is the lowest in the set by a wide margin, so the one-week band is correspondingly narrow. The stance is Sell, and the flip level to Hold sits exactly at the current level, meaning any advance at all reverses it. The confidence figure is worth stating plainly: the Sell stance has historically been correct less than half the time in the pooled backtest, so this is the weakest-evidenced stance on the page and should be read as a caution flag rather than a forecast.
words.macro: The index finished roughly flat on the week in a session mix that favoured large-cap technology over rate-sensitive cyclicals and smaller companies. The Fed's first hike in three years, delivered on a unanimous vote with a signal of more to come, lifted the median end-year policy rate projection to about 4.1% from 3.8% in June, and the ten-year Treasury yield spent the week pressing toward 5%. That combination — an index near the top of its range against a discount rate that is rising rather than falling — is the tension the defensive stance is registering. The September employment report on 2 October and September CPI on 14 October fall inside the one-month horizon and are the scheduled tests of whether the tightening path priced this week survives contact with the data.
words.long_term: The index's medium-term strength continues to rest on earnings concentrated in a small number of very large companies, which makes the aggregate more robust than the average constituent but also more exposed to any repricing of that narrow group. The standing question is whether a higher resting level of policy rates permanently lowers the multiple the market is willing to pay.

eoy_scenarios.central: The central band assumes earnings hold up well enough to absorb a higher discount rate, leaving the index grinding within a narrow range into year-end rather than making a decisive move in either direction.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The upside case is a soft inflation path that lets the Fed stop after one or two more moves, releasing the valuation pressure while growth stays intact.
eoy_scenarios.downside: The downside case is the hawkish path being taken literally — further hikes, the ten-year yield settling above 5%, and multiple compression that a high starting range position leaves little cushion against.

Range position near 0.87 is high, just below the broad index, so the starting point is an extended one. The stance is Hold, flipping to Flat near 29073, which leaves a meaningful buffer of roughly two percent below current levels before the reading changes.
words.macro: Technology outperformed on the week, with the tech-heavy indices gaining while rate-sensitive cyclicals and smaller companies lagged — a rotation into selected large-cap technology exposure rather than a broad advance. That is a notable outcome given that long-duration growth assets are theoretically the most exposed to the yield backdrop, with the ten-year approaching 5% after the Fed's hike and its signal of further tightening. The reasonable reading is that investors are treating the largest technology earnings streams as defensive in a slowing economy, which works until either those earnings disappoint or the yield move becomes disorderly.
words.long_term: The structural case remains the reinvestment of very large operating cash flows into compute capacity and the returns expected from it, and the concentration that produces is both the strength and the fragility of the index. The standing risk is not that the technology case fails but that the capital intensity required to pursue it compresses the free cash flow the valuations assume.

eoy_scenarios.central: The central band assumes the current rotation holds — large technology earnings continuing to justify their premium while higher rates cap further multiple expansion — leaving the index drifting near current levels into year-end.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The upside case is an earnings season that validates the capital spending, combined with any softening in the rate path that lets long-duration assets re-rate.
eoy_scenarios.downside: The downside case is a genuine yield shock or a disappointment from one of the handful of companies that dominate the index, either of which would find a market already positioned near the top of its twelve-month range.

words.technical: The trend composite of roughly 0.43 is dominated by the one-month reading, which at about 1.06 is the strongest short-horizon figure in the set — this is a move that happened recently and quickly, not a slow accumulation. The three-month reading is still negative, so the longer picture has not caught up. Range position near 0.74 sits in the upper third of the past year. Daily volatility of about 0.31% is by far the lowest of the seven instruments, which is why the bands are so tight in percentage terms. The stance is Hold, with the flip level to Flat sitting exactly at the current level — the reading is finely balanced and a single quiet session could change it.
words.macro: The index rose around 1.1% for its best week in about three months and topped 100 for the first time since July, after the Fed's unanimous quarter-point hike and a dot plot showing a higher rate path than markets had assumed — the median end-year projection moved to roughly 4.1% from 3.8% in June. The rate differential argument did the work: the decision removed what had been the main impediment to a stronger dollar, and other major currencies weakened against it through the week. The index also briefly cleared its 200-day moving average, a technical marker widely watched as a continuation signal, though its predictive value should not be overstated.
words.long_term: The dollar's standing support is the depth of its markets and its role as the default settlement and reserve currency, which makes demand for it relatively insensitive to the rate cycle. The slow structural counterweight is gradual reserve diversification, which moves on a timescale of years and has never yet shown up as a decisive force in any single quarter.

eoy_scenarios.central: The central band assumes the rate differential that drove this week's move persists without widening much further, leaving the index holding recent gains in a narrow range into year-end.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The upside case is the Fed delivering the additional hikes it signalled while other major central banks stay on hold or ease, widening the gap that currency markets trade.
eoy_scenarios.downside: The downside case is inflation cooling quickly enough that the signalled path is not delivered, unwinding a move that was built almost entirely on one week's repricing of expectations.

coherence.note: The dollar and crude carry the same Hold stance this week even though their documented relationship is negative, because the two were driven by separate forces rather than by each other: the dollar rose on a hawkish policy surprise, while oil fell on the unwinding of a specific physical supply fear, and a supply-side move in crude does not have to show up as a mirror image in the currency.

week_summary: The week was defined by a central-bank turn: the Federal Reserve raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00%, its first increase in three years, and signalled that more tightening could follow this year. The dollar had its strongest week in months and long Treasury yields pressed toward 5%. Crude went the other way, giving back a chunk of the previous week's supply-shock premium as Saudi shuttle shipments and talk of a quicker pipeline restart cooled fears of a lasting disruption; the retreat in oil in turn pulled yields back off their highs late in the week and let precious metals recover. Equities finished mixed, with large-cap technology outperforming rate-sensitive and smaller names. The model reads five of seven instruments as Hold or Flat, with only the S&P 500 in a defensive stance, and the pooled backtest is a reminder to hold that one lightly: the Sell stance has historically been right less than half the time, while Flat is by far the best-evidenced stance in the set.
